ETAS: a self-exciting process with marks and the Omori law

Source: R/mhk.R
etasf.Rd

Fits the temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence (ETAS) model of Ogata (1988) to event times with marks (a magnitude, the number of victims, the severity of an incident): $$\lambda(t) = \mu + K \sum_{t_j < t} e^{\alpha (m_j - m_0)} (t - t_j + c)^{-p},$$ so bigger events trigger more, and the triggering decays as a power of the time since (the modified Omori law). Without marks, or with constant ones, \(\alpha\) is fixed at 0 and the model is a Hawkes process with a Lomax kernel (that of hwkfit() with shape \(p - 1\) and scale \(c\)). The log-likelihood over [0, hor] is maximised with its analytic gradient by BFGS over the logarithms of \(\mu\), \(K\), \(c\) and \(p - 1\) (and \(\alpha\)), from two starts or start; standard errors from the numerical Hessian of the gradient. branch is the branching ratio \(K \bar{e^{\alpha (m - m_0)}} c^{1 - p} / (p - 1)\), the mean number of events each event triggers. On data with little power-law tail the likelihood rises towards the exponential limit of the kernel (c and p growing together): the fit then stops with conv FALSE, and hwkfit()'s exponential kernel is the better model.

Usage

etasf(times, hor, mag = NULL, m0 = NULL, start = NULL, maxit = 500)

Arguments

times

Event times: numbers sorted in [0, hor], at least 10.

hor

The end of the window: one positive number.

mag

NULL or the mark of each event: finite numbers.

m0

NULL (the least mark) or the reference mark: one number.

start

NULL or the starting mu, k, alpha, c and p.

maxit

The most BFGS steps per start: one whole number from 1.

Value

An object of class etasf, a list: par, se and cov of (mu, k, alpha, c, p; alpha's are NA when it is fixed); loglik, aic; branch; conv, iter; afree, whether alpha was estimated; n and hor.

References

Ogata, Y. (1988). Statistical models for earthquake occurrences and residual analysis for point processes. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 83(401), 9-27. doi:10.1080/01621459.1988.10478560

See also

hwkfit(), mvhwk(), sthwk().

Examples

x <- hwksim(c(log(0.3), 0.5, 0.6, 1), 800, kernel = "lomax", seed = 5)
etasf(x$t, 800)
#> etasf: 530 events in [0, 800]; no marks, alpha fixed at 0
#>             est         se
#> mu    0.3327782 0.08931391
#> k     0.4373506 0.87721720
#> alpha 0.0000000         NA
#> c     1.3824477 1.65692065
#> p     1.6791760 0.82290541
#> branching ratio 0.5167995; log-likelihood -724.0694, AIC 1456.139
